## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Speech Technology for Conversational AI
  Code                    M2 · P2 (announced) — official code not published (course description not published)
  Team and workload       Instructor: master's team · \~24 h · building the complete voice loop — signal (Mel spectrogram/MFCC), ASR from GMM-HMM to CTC (loss derived), LAS, Whisper and streaming, TTS from the vocoder (WaveNet, HiFi-GAN) to diffusion/flow models, expressivity and cloning (ethics, audio watermarking), up to full-duplex conversational voices and speech LLMs — the bridge between Signal Processing (M1) and LLMs (M2).
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2}[Outside the recommended track]{.badge .position} · M2 program being finalized
  ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an NLP / signal engineer who wants the full voice loop. **Empirical first**: WER 4% in studio → 28% on noisy phone; TTS that clones a voice with no watermark — then we name Mel, CTC, Whisper, vocoders.

ASR → TTS → speech LLMs: bridge from Signal Processing (M1) to LLMs (M2).

### What you will be able to do

-   Choose and compute the representations of the speech signal (Mel spectrogram, MFCC) according to the use;
-   Explain the classical GMM-HMM pipeline and what caused its replacement;
-   Derive the CTC loss (sum over alignments, forward-backward) and implement it;
-   Compare LAS, Conformer and RNN-T according to the quality/latency trade-off, and explain Whisper's multi-task robustness;
-   Size a streaming system: chunking, voice activity detection, latency vs quality;
-   Explain the modern TTS chain: vocoders (WaveNet to HiFi-GAN), Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow approaches;
-   Control the expressivity of a synthesis (prosody, style tokens, SSML) and master the ethical issues of voice cloning;
-   Describe the complete conversational loop (VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex) and how multilingual speech LLMs work.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module offered in period 2, outside the recommended track: it is the master's "multimodal" module devoted to the audio modality, designed as the joint production deployment of two prerequisites. **Prerequisites**: [Signal Processing](../m1p1-signal-processing/index.html) (windowing, Fourier transform, spectrograms — revisited in ch. 0) and [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html), whose multimodal chapter (ch. 8) announces the speech LLMs covered here at the end of the course.

**Downstream**: the module gives its voice component to the conversational assistant — the LLGA's application through-line, which crosses the agents of [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html) (ch. 8) and the production constraints of [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (P99 latency, costs); it also extends the watermarking of the [Control in Generative AI](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html) module to the audio side.

### Course outline

-   **Recap: the speech signal and its representations** — windowing, Mel spectrograms and MFCC: the raw material of the whole course.
-   **Classical ASR: the GMM-HMM pipeline** — the historical architecture, still useful to understand what neural methods replaced.
-   **CTC: the loss, derived** — learning without frame/phoneme alignment: the complete derivation of the loss that opened up deep ASR.
-   **Encoder-decoder: LAS, Conformer, RNN-T** — three architectural answers to the quality/latency trade-off.
-   **Whisper: robustness and multi-task** — what very large-scale supervised learning changes (and costs).
-   **Streaming: chunking, VAD, latency vs quality** — going from file to stream: split, detect speech, own the latency.
-   **Vocoders: from WaveNet to HiFi-GAN** — generating the waveform itself, and the path from slow autoregressive models to fast GANs.
-   **Neural TTS: Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow** — modern synthesis from text to spectrogram then to signal.
-   **Expressivity: prosody, style tokens, SSML** — not only saying, but *how* to say it.
-   **Voice conversion and cloning: ethics and watermarking** — the promises of cloning, its misuse, and how to mark generated audio.
-   **The conversational loop: VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex** — listening, waiting one's turn, interrupting oneself: real-time orchestration.
-   **Speech LLMs and multilingualism** — the speech signal fed directly into the language model: architectures and issues for low-resource languages.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — align a CTC, measure a WER, synthesize and watermark a voice clip.
-   **References** — the founding papers of neural ASR and TTS.

### How to study this module

-   Listen to every example audio of the course (originals, degraded, synthesized): the ear is here a measuring instrument to train as much as the WER.
-   Write the CTC forward-backward yourself on a mini-example by hand: it is the obligatory step to never again confuse alignment and decoding.
-   For each architecture, place it on the "latency/quality" axis and note what is computed online versus offline: it is the module's reading grid.
-   Wire up a mini "microphone → ASR → response → TTS → speaker" loop early, even a basic one, then improve it chapter after chapter.
-   Read ch. 9 (cloning, ethics) with the eye of a future professional: questions of consent and audio watermarking will arise in your projects from the internship onward.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} With speech LLMs, voice has become a first-class modality for language models: the LLGA master, which trains at the crossroads of LLMs and their applications, offers you here the complete chain — from spectrogram to speaking turn — rather than a simple overview. Conversational assistants (telephony, accessibility, embedded voice interfaces) are one of the most in-demand career paths in the field, and the module crosses all the master's skills: signal, LLMs, real-time streaming, ethics and control.
:::

## 0. Recap: the speech signal and its representations {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (Signal Processing M1 module) — what is assumed known
:::

-   **Sampling** (ch. 4): Shannon's theorem; speech is sampled at 16 kHz (ASR) or 24 kHz (synthesis), useful telephone band 300-3400 Hz, formants up to \~8 kHz;
-   **Time-frequency analysis** (ch. 6): STFT, Gabor windows, time-frequency trade-off — *the* spectrogram is the input of almost all the models in this module (cf. Signal Processing module ch. 6);
-   **Mel spectrogram and MFCC** (ch. 8): 25 ms frames every 10 ms, Hann window, Mel filter bank (perceptual scale linear below 1 kHz then logarithmic: $m = 2595\log_{10}(1 + f/700)$), 20-80 coefficients, possibly DCT (MFCC);
-   **Random signals** (ch. 7): power spectral density, periodogram — used by energy-based VADs (ch. 10) and spread-spectrum watermarking (ch. 9);
-   **Recurrent networks and transformers** (Deep Learning M1): LSTM, attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})V$ — the ASR/TTS encoder is a transformer (ch. 3-4);
-   **Diffusion and VAE** (Multimodal GenAI M1 ch. 1 and 3): ELBO, DDPM, noise prediction — the generative TTS models (ch. 7) descend directly from them.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — ASR and TTS, formalized]{.tag} **Recognition** (ASR): estimate the transcription $y$ (sequence of tokens — characters, phonemes, BPE) of an acoustic frame $x_{1:T}$ (Mel features, typically $T \approx 100$ frames for 10 s of speech): model $p_\theta(y \mid x_{1:T})$. **Synthesis** (TTS): the inverse, $p_\theta(x \mid y)$ — a *one-to-many* problem: a text can be said in infinitely many ways (voice, rate, emotion), which will structure all of ch. 7-8 (TTS is a *generation* problem, ASR a *decision* problem). The reference ASR error is the **WER**: $$\mathrm{WER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N},$$ substitutions/deletions/insertions obtained by word-level Levenshtein alignment between hypothesis and reference (lab 1).
:::

::: note
[The module's line — and why "conversational"]{.tag} The course follows the stack of a voice assistant: understand (ch. 1-5), speak (ch. 6-9), converse (ch. 10-11). The technical thread: two *breaks* occurred — (i) the abandonment of explicit alignment (HMM → CTC → attention → discrete tokens); (ii) the fusion of the three ASR+LLM+TTS building blocks into a single multimodal model (speech LLMs, ch. 11) that speaks and listens — where *full-duplex* conversation (ch. 10) becomes computable. Speech regains its status there: the fastest (3-4 words/s produced, 5-8 understood) and most natural interface.
:::

::: note
[Module status]{.tag} Course proposed in the M2 brochure (period 2): the instructors are not yet confirmed; there is therefore no "research of the instructor" chapter — the content follows the standards of the field and constantly builds on the modules already covered (Signal Processing M1 for the signal, LLMs M2 for the language layer).
:::

## 1. Classical ASR: the GMM-HMM pipeline {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a business ASR fine-tuned on call-center audio drops as soon as the accent changes. This chapter sets signal representation and decoding objectives.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Ignoring acoustic domain; evaluating WER alone (no semantics); voice cloning without ethical guardrails / watermarking.
:::

The historical pipeline (1980-2015) survives only as technical memories — but its formalism (emission model, chain of states, Bayesian decoding) reappears everywhere, up to the CTC forward-backward (ch. 2). We cover it in one structured chapter.

::: thm
[Theorem 1.1 — The GMM-HMM acoustic model and decoding]{.tag} One decomposes $p(x_{1:T} \mid w)$ with a hidden Markov chain over phonetic states $q_t$: each phoneme is a 3-state left-to-right HMM (beginning/middle/end), put in context (triphones); the emission of a state is a **Gaussian mixture** over the MFCCs (39 dimensions: 13 + first and second derivatives): $$p(x_t \mid q_t = s) = \sum_{m=1}^{M_s} c_{sm}\, \mathcal N(x_t;\ \mu_{sm}, \Sigma_{sm}),$$ and the retained transcription maximizes *Bayesian decoding* $$\hat w = \arg\max_w\ p(x_{1:T} \mid w)\, p_{\mathrm{LM}}(w),$$ where $p_{\mathrm{LM}}$ is an n-gram language model (cf. NLP M1 module ch. 2). The likelihood is computed by the *forward* recursion $$\alpha_t(j) = \Big[\sum_i \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\Big]\, b_j(x_t),$$ ($\mathcal O(T N^2)$, $N$ states) and the best path by *Viterbi* (same recursion, max instead of the sum). Training: EM (Baum-Welch) — cf. Graph ML M1 module ch. 5 for the EM of latent-variable models.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Why GMM? And why is it dead?]{.tag} (i) A Gaussian mixture is a universal density approximator (with enough components, any continuous density is approximated): it was the best parameterization *before* deep learning. (ii) Fatal flaws: MFCCs are not semantic features (the GMM models acoustic blocks, knows nothing about similar phones); the HMM assumes the signal locally stationary per state and conditional independence of the frames; above all, each piece (lexicon, contexts, LM) is optimized separately — impossible to align globally. Neural systems *eat* raw data: 10,000 labeled hours replace 300 carefully curated ones (ch. 4).
:::

::: note
[What survives of the pipeline]{.tag} Three direct legacies: (i) the acoustic + LM *fusion* at decoding (the "shallow fusion" reappears with LLMs to rescore N-bests); (ii) the *forward-backward* — the central algorithm of CTC in the next chapter; (iii) *forced alignment* (finding the instants of each word, still used for subtitling and training TTS). Historical reference: Rabiner's tutorial (Proc. IEEE, 1989) remains a limpid read.
:::

## 2. CTC: the loss, derived {#ch2}

The central problem of neural ASR: the output (sequence of tokens $y$) is shorter than the input ($T$ frames) and *unaligned* — there is no label per frame. The solution of Graves et al. (ICML 2006): marginalize over *all* possible alignments. We derive everything: this is technical chapter no. 1 of the module.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Alignments and collapse]{.tag} The network emits at each frame a distribution $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x_{1:T}, t)$ over the extended alphabet $\mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\}$ ($\epsilon$ = blank). A *path* $\pi \in (\mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\})^T$ is a sequence of $T$ symbols, drawn independently: $p(\pi \mid x) = \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(\pi_t \mid x, t)$. The **collapse** map $\mathcal B$ first removes the blanks then merges consecutive repetitions: $\mathcal B(\texttt{hh ee ll ll o}) = \texttt{helo}$ (the three consecutive l's, once the blanks are removed, make only one). Conversely, doubles *separated by a blank* survive: $\mathcal B(\texttt{l}\,\epsilon\,\texttt{l}) = \texttt{ll}$ — that is the whole art of CTC. The CTC loss marginalizes: $$p_\theta(y \mid x) \;=\; \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal B^{-1}(y)} p(\pi \mid x), \qquad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CTC}} = -\log p_\theta(y \mid x).$$ *Why the blank is indispensable*: without it, a collapsed $\texttt{ll}$ could not be distinguished from $\texttt{l}$ — impossible to write "bonne" with a double n. The blank carries the boundary information.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.2 — Counting by hand (T = 4, y = "ab")]{.tag} Extended sequence $\ell = (\epsilon, a, \epsilon, b)$ (length $S = 4$). The valid paths of length 4 are: $aa\epsilon b$? No — let us enumerate seriously: $\texttt{-a-b}$, $\texttt{-ab-}$, $\texttt{a--b}$, $\texttt{a-b-}$, $\texttt{aa-b}$, $\texttt{a-ab}$, $\texttt{-aab}$, $\texttt{ab--}$ (8 paths). Each contributes its product of 4 probabilities: $p(y\|x)$ is the sum of the 8; exercise 3 computes it for numerical values, exercise 4 checks with the implementation. The number of paths grows exponentially ($\sim \|\mathcal V\|^T$): direct summation is impossible — hence the forward-backward.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — CTC forward-backward (recursions and gradient, proven)]{.tag} Let $p_t(k) = p_\theta(k \mid x, t)$, and $\ell$ the extended sequence. The *forward variables* $\alpha_t(s) = p(\ell_{1:s} \text{ reached at frame } t)$ follow $$\alpha_t(s) = \Big[\alpha_{t-1}(s) + \alpha_{t-1}(s{-}1) + \mathbf 1\{\ell_s \neq \epsilon,\ \ell_s \neq \ell_{s-2}\}\, \alpha_{t-1}(s{-}2)\Big]\cdot p_t(\ell_s),$$ initialized $\alpha_1(1) = p_1(\epsilon)$, $\alpha_1(2) = p_1(\ell_2)$, the rest at 0 (one cannot "jump" ahead). Symmetrically $\beta_t(s)$ (backward, from the end). Then $$p(y \mid x) = \alpha_T(S) + \alpha_T(S{-}1), \qquad \alpha_t(s)\,\beta_t(s) = p\big(y \mid x,\ \pi_t = \ell_s\big)\cdot p_t(\ell_s),$$ and the gradient of the loss is written in closed form $$\frac{\partial \mathcal L_{\mathrm{CTC}}}{\partial p_t(k)} = -\,\frac{1}{p(y \mid x)}\ \frac{1}{p_t(k)} \sum_{s\,:\,\ell_s = k} \alpha_t(s)\, \beta_t(s).$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (decomposition by the state at $t$).** The sum over paths partitions according to the position $s$ occupied at frame $t$: each path passing through $\ell_s$ at $t$ factorizes into "prefix reaching $\ell_s$ at $t$" $\times$ "$p_t(\ell_s)$" $\times$ "suffix from $\ell_s$ at $t{+}1$" — hence $\alpha_t(s)\beta_t(s) = p(y, \pi_t = \ell_s \mid x)$ (careful: the definition of $\beta$ includes the $p_t$ factor or not depending on the convention; with the one above, $\alpha_t(s)$ contains $p_t(\ell_s)$ and $\beta_t(s)$ does not). **Step 2 (recursion).** For the path to be at $\ell_s$ at $t$, it was at $s$, $s{-}1$ or $s{-}2$ at $t{-}1$; the jump of two positions is forbidden *except* if $\ell_s$ is a real letter different from $\ell_{s-2}$ (otherwise two identical letters would be merged by the collapse; and one never jumps *over* a letter). **Step 3 (gradient).** $p(y\|x) = \sum_{\pi} \prod_{t'} p_{t'}(\pi_{t'})$; each term using $p_t(k)$ corresponds to the paths with $\pi_t = k \in \ell$, whose total sum equals $\sum_{s:\ell_s = k}\alpha_t(s)\beta_t(s)$. Differentiating the log: $\partial \mathcal L/\partial p_t(k) = -\partial p(y\|x)/\partial p_t(k) \cdot 1/p(y\|x)$, and $\partial p(y\|x)/\partial p_t(k) = \big[\sum_s \alpha\beta\big] / p_t(k)$ (each path where $\pi_t = k$ is linear in $p_t(k)$). **Complexity**: $\mathcal O(T \cdot S)$ — two tables of $T \times (2\|y\|+1)$, versus the exponential enumeration. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — CTC inference and model assumptions]{.tag} (i) *Greedy decoding*: $\hat y = \mathcal B(\arg\max_k p_t(k)\ \text{for each } t)$ — fast, suboptimal; *beam search*: maintain $K$ prefixes with their truncated $\alpha$ scores, merge equal prefixes after collapse, optionally rescored by an LM. (ii) *Assumptions of CTC*: conditional independence of the frames (no internal language model — hence the external LM) and *monotone* distribution (the alignment goes left to right): perfect for reading, forbidden for translation (ch. 3 to break free of it).
:::

::: note
[CTC's posterity]{.tag} CTC lives everywhere in 2026: forced alignment (lab 1), the pre-training of wav2vec 2 (CTC objective), and — above all — **RNN-T** (ch. 3) is a CTC extended to real time, with a blank reinterpreted as "move forward in time". By contrast, Whisper is *not* CTC (attention encoder-decoder, ch. 4): knowing how to say "this one marginalizes alignments, that one generates them" is a classic oral-exam question.
:::

## 3. Encoder-decoder: LAS, Conformer, RNN-T {#ch3}

::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — LAS: Listen, Attend and Spell (Chan et al., ICASSP 2016)]{.tag} **Listen**: a pyramidal BLSTM (then transformer) encoder compacts the frames $x_{1:T}$ into states $h_j$. **Attend**: at each output step $i$, an additive attention computes $$e_{ij} = v^\top \tanh\big(W_s s_{i-1} + W_h h_j\big), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_{j'} \exp e_{ij'}}, \qquad c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij}\, h_j,$$ (*location-sensitive* attention in practice: the past weights $a_{i-1}$ enter $e_{ij}$ to make it monotone and avoid skipped/repeated words). **Spell**: an autoregressive decoder emits $y_i$ from $(s_{i-1}, y_{i-1}, c_i)$, trained by teacher forcing and cross-entropy. The loss is no longer a marginalization: the attention *learns* the alignment — and can reorder it (used for speech translation). Two inherited weaknesses: *exposure bias* (trained on the reference, tested on its own errors) and the impossibility of strict streaming (all of $x$ is read before the first token).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Conformer: local convolution + global attention (Gulati et al., Interspeech 2020)]{.tag} The Conformer block chains ("macaron" style) two feed-forward networks with a 1/2 factor around *(i)* a multi-head attention with *relative* positional encoding (captures long context — sentences span hundreds of frames) and *(ii)* a deep convolutional module (pointwise convolution $ \to $ depthwise with dilation, GLU/SiLU, LayerNorm) that captures local phonetics (formants, transitions). The takeaway intuition: attention alone is bad at the fine local patterns of speech, convolution alone does not see the context — the sandwich of the two dominated industrial ASR 2021-2024 (before being absorbed by the foundation models of ch. 4: wav2vec 2, HuBERT, Whisper encoder).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — RNN-T (Graves, 2012): the CTC that speaks in real time]{.tag} The RNN-transducer combines an *encoder* $f_t$ (frame $\to$ state, causal — processed on the fly) and a *prediction network* $g_u$ (tokens already emitted $\to$ state); a joint network produces $$P(k \mid t, u) = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W\, f_t + W'\, g_u + b\big)_{k}, \qquad k \in \mathcal V \cup \{\epsilon\},$$ and the likelihood sums over all paths of the $(t, u)$ grid — it is the forward-backward of Theorem 2.3, transposed onto a $T \times U$ trellis where $\epsilon$ = "advance in $t$ without emitting". Decisive property: the encoder is *causal*, each $f_t$ is computable as soon as the frame arrives — RNN-T is the queen architecture of **streaming** ASR (ch. 5), notably on device. Cost: an $\mathcal O(TU)$ lattice at training and the CTC monotonicity assumption (no reordering).
:::

  Architecture      Alignment                Loss                       Streaming           Internal LM?               Typical use
  ----------------- ------------------------ -------------------------- ------------------- -------------------------- --------------------------------
  GMM-HMM (ch. 1)   explicit states          EM (Baum-Welch)            yes                 no (n-gram)                legacy, old telephony
  CTC (ch. 2)       marginalized, monotone   forward-backward           partial             no                         forced alignment, pre-training
  LAS (ch. 3)       learned (attention)      cross-entropy              no                  yes (AR decoder)           offline, max quality
  RNN-T (ch. 3)     monotone trellis         2D forward-backward        yes                 partial (prediction net)   assistants, mobile
  Whisper (ch. 4)   generated (attention)    multi-task cross-entropy   no (30 s windows)   yes                        general transcription

## 4. Whisper: robustness and multi-task {#ch4}

::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Whisper (Radford et al., ICML 2023): the strength of the weak]{.tag} Trained on $\approx$ 680,000 hours of *weakly supervised* audio/text pairs collected from the web (versus a few hundred to thousand carefully curated hours before), Whisper is a simple transformer encoder-decoder (88M-1.5B parameters); the audio is cut into 30 s windows, log-Mel 80 bins. The output is a *sequence of special tokens + text*: $\langle\!\|$start$\,\|\rangle \to$ language $\to$ task (transcribe/translate into English) $\to$ timestamps $\to$ text — everything (language identifier, translation decision, time) is *learned as language*, no dedicated module. Results: unprecedented robustness to noise/reverberation/accents (trained on real, not read data), WER close to humans on clean English; best zero-shot performance on most languages at the time.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Why it works: the scaling law of dirty data]{.tag} (i) *Coverage*: robustness is not a module, it is a consequence of diversity — the 680 kh cover real-world mess (background noise, music, accents), whereas LibriSpeech (1000 h of read books) overlearns clean reading; (ii) *Filtering beats labeling*: the training pipeline filters aggressively (language detection, audio-text matching by an initial ASR, anti-hallucination heuristics) rather than correcting by hand — the *moderately clean but massive* data wins; (iii) *Multi-task as regularization*: transcribing AND translating AND timestamping share one encoder — translation forces semantic, not only acoustic, representations. Documented limits: hallucinations on long silences (looped repetitions — the model "invents" text), no native streaming (ch. 5), difficult fine specialization.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — French in the crosshairs]{.tag} On clean English, a good system reaches human WER (\~5%); the same model on spontaneous contemporary French typically does 2 to 3 times worse (accents, speaking rates, code-switching, proper names) — lab 1 measures it. Three French phenomena to know for engineering: *liaison* (les\|ami·z·arbitres: spelling is not phonetics — the ASR must relearn the graphy), *enchaînement* (final consonant tied to the next vowel: word boundaries blur in the spectrogram) and *number verbalization* (1996: "mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-seize" or "dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-seize"? — normalization ambiguity, both are valid; cf. ch. 8 for the reverse direction in TTS).
:::

## 5. Streaming: chunking, VAD, latency vs quality {#ch5}

Conversing means answering fast: the ASR must produce words *while* one speaks. This chapter deals with the "offline $\to$ streaming" transformation, whose cost is measured in WER added per second gained.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Latencies of a streaming ASR]{.tag} The **algorithmic latency** of a chunked encoder (*chunking*) of size $L$ frames with a lookahead of $R$ frames equals $$\lambda = (L + R)\,\Delta, \qquad \Delta = \text{frame step } (10\ \mathrm{ms}),$$ — one cannot predict before having heard the context. The **real-time factor** (RTF) measures the computational cost: computation time / audio duration (RTF $<$ 1 required, $<<$ 1 on device). The **first-word latency** adds the VAD (ch. 10) and the energy bar. A conversational voice assistant targets $\lambda \leq 300$ ms end to end (lab 5) — humans answer in \~200 ms (ch. 10): this is *the* structuring constraint of the field.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Three streaming architectures (Moritz et al., ICASSP 2020, for the first)]{.tag}

1.  **Block attention**: the transformer encoder processes windows of $L$ frames with a complete left context (memory) and a bounded right lookahead $R$ — the attention is *masked* beyond; the larger $R$ grows, the more the WER drops and the latency rises (curve of ch. 5.3);
2.  **Causal RNN-T** (Theorem 3.3): pure encoder $L = 1$, $R = 0$ — emission from the frame on; the lookahead is reinjected into the *prediction* network (the right context comes from the tokens already emitted); standard on mobile;
3.  **Asynchronous re-scoring**: a first streaming pass gives the real-time display, an offline model (Whisper) *re-corrects* the final transcription with a few hundred ms of delay — the interface shows the text "correcting itself" (the design of 2026 assistants: the truth arrives one second later, reactivity is immediate).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — The latency/quality curve, and how to read it]{.tag} For each point $(L, R)$ (or each model choice): measure WER and first-word latency on a *fixed* test corpus; plot WER($\lambda$). Typical shape: plateau up to $\lambda \approx 200$ ms (the useful context of a phoneme fits in \~200 ms), then rapid drop (one loses the transitions), then plateau (ultra-context no longer helps). Engineer's reading: choose the elbow point; scientific reading: the curve *is* a control curve (fidelity against resource) — exactly the grid of the Control in Generative AI module (M2, ch. 2 and 9), where "diversity" is replaced by "reactivity".
:::

::: note
[VAD: the gateway of the stream]{.tag} *Voice activity detection* decides, window by window (10-30 ms), whether the frame contains speech: energy + periodicity (historical), energy/noise GMM (Signal module ch. 7), lightweight networks (Silero VAD — the lab's tool). Two errors of opposite cost: the *false alarm* sends noise to the ASR (Whisper hallucinations on silences!); the *miss* cuts word beginnings (the initial French "euh"). The VAD also initiates *endpointing* — deciding that the user has finished speaking (ch. 10): even more sensitive, because it sets the *perceived* latency of the whole system.
:::

## 6. Vocoders: from WaveNet to HiFi-GAN {#ch6}

::: thm
[Theorem 6.1 — WaveNet (van den Oord et al., 2016): autoregression over the samples]{.tag} The vocoder models the waveform directly: $$p(x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T_{\mathrm{ech}}} p(x_t \mid x_{<t},\, c),$$ with $T_{\mathrm{ech}}$ = 24,000 samples per second, $x_t$ $\mu$-law quantized over 256 levels, $c$ the conditioning (Mel, speaker). Architecture: **dilated causal convolutions** — layer $k$ looks $2^k$ samples back (dilations 1, 2, 4, ..., 512, stacked): the receptive field grows *exponentially* with depth ($\approx 2^L$ for $L$ layers), where a non-dilated convolution would require $2^L$ layers. Quality: close to human speech in subjective tests (MOS above 4, versus \~4.5 for the ground truth); fatal flaw: generating one second of speech takes 24,000 sequential steps — orders of magnitude slower than real time, unusable in production.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — HiFi-GAN (Kong et al., NeurIPS 2020): speed through the adversary]{.tag} Complete reversal: the generator is *parallel feed-forward* (upsampling by transposed convolutions from the 80-bin Mel to the waveform, then multi-receptive-field dilated convolutions for phase coherence); training is *adversarial* (GAN recap: Multimodal GenAI M1 module ch. 2) with two families of discriminators — *multi-period* (they rearrange the waveform into matrices of periods 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 to trap periodic artifacts: the "buzz") and *multi-scale* — plus an L1 loss on the reconstructed Mel to anchor the content. Result: WaveNet quality, parallel generation — orders of magnitude faster than real time on GPU, the industry's default vocoder. To remember from the chapter: the pairing of *mixing duration* (autoregressive over 24 kHz) *against parallel architecture + perceptual loss* dictates all of modern TTS.
:::

::: note
[The Mel as a contractual interface]{.tag} The two stages of the TTS (ch. 7) communicate via the Mel spectrogram: 80 bins, one frame roughly every 12 ms (\~ 80 Hz), logarithmic scale — the vocoder's *specification sheet*. Changing the definition (sampling frequency, hop, n_bins) breaks the model/vocoder compatibility — the first experiment of lab 2. And the Mel is not invertible (phase lost): the whole difficulty of the vocoder is to *re-invent* a coherent phase — hence the period discriminators.
:::

## 7. Neural TTS: Tacotron 2, VITS, diffusion and flow {#ch7}

::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Tacotron 2 (Shen et al., ICASSP 2018): the two-stage scheme]{.tag} Stage 1 (acrobatic): an *attentional* encoder-decoder reads the text (graphemes) and writes the Mel frame by frame — the *location-sensitive* attention learns the text→acoustic alignment there (same mechanism as LAS in ch. 3, applied in reverse); training by teacher forcing on the reference Mels. Stage 2: a WaveNet (ch. 6) turns the Mel into a wave. Historical quality: natural on read sentences. Two chronic diseases: *attention failure* (skipped or stuttered words on long or out-of-distribution sentences) and *abusive determinization* — one text, a single voice/rate (the one-to-many of Definition 0.1 denied by training toward the *average* Mel: smoothed, metallic output).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — VITS (Kim et al., ICML 2021): one-stage, stochastic, end-to-end]{.tag} Three ideas that answer Tacotron's diseases. *(i) VAE:* a variational encoder encodes the target speech into $z$; the decoder (HiFi-GAN) writes the wave from $z$ — the *noise* of the prior explores the multiplicity of ways of saying; *(ii) normalizing flow:* a flow (exact change of variables: cf. Graph Generative Models M2 module ch. 4 for the proof) aligns the distribution of the text-conditioned latent with the prior, which makes training end-to-end (exact likelihood + adversary); *(iii) implicit monotone alignment* (MAS: search for the optimal monotone alignment between text and Mel, refined at each step). Result: a single text→wave network, parallel, stochastic — the first "industrializable" generation of TTS (YourTTS, ch. 9, derives from it).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 7.3 — Iterative generation arrives: Grad-TTS then Voicebox]{.tag} **Grad-TTS (Popov et al., ICML 2021)**: an encoder predicts, for each phone, the *target mean* $\mu(x)$ of a Gaussian in Mel space; a *diffusion* decoder (DDPM — cf. Multimodal GenAI M1 module ch. 3) turns a noise $\mathcal N(0, I)$ into a Mel around $\mu$, guided by the noise prediction $\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \mu)$; a duration predictor handles the number of frames per phone. Quality grows with the number of steps... like latency: the step/quality curve is *the* trade-off curve of the Control module (M2) ch. 9, in TTS version. **Voicebox (Le et al., 2023)**: *conditional flow matching in infilling mode* — one masks a region of the Mel and regenerates *only it*, the context remaining fixed: the same machinery as DiGress's inpainting (Graph Generative Models M2 module ch. 5) transported into acoustics. Immediate applications: editing a word in a sentence while keeping the voice, de-noising, voice translation... and zero-shot cloning from a few seconds of reference. Non-autoregressive and parallel: the dominant family of research TTS 2024-2026.
:::

  System                 Paradigm                    Alignment             Stochastic?           Streaming          Native cloning
  ---------------------- --------------------------- --------------------- --------------------- ------------------ ----------------------------
  Tacotron 2 + WaveNet   AR attention + AR vocoder   learned attention     no                    no                 no
  VITS                   VAE + flow + GAN            implicit MAS          yes (prior)           difficult          via speaker emb. (YourTTS)
  Grad-TTS               diffusion to Mel            predicted durations   yes (initial noise)   per step           no
  Voicebox               flow matching, infilling    none (conditioned)    yes                   region by region   yes (3 s prompt)

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Latency budget of a conversational TTS]{.tag} Goal: < 300 ms between the end of the LLM's decision and the first sound. An AR Tacotron-like: the first *sentence* must be synthesized before the first sound (if one wants the intonation) — 1-2 s of lead time required: prohibitive. VITS: the first *chunk* of Mel (a few frames) suffices — \~100 ms; Voicebox: one must bound the number of sampling steps: 4-10 steps (instead of 50-100) with distillation, otherwise quality drops (the curve of thm. 7.3). Conclusion: the full-duplex of ch. 10 was only possible after the non-autoregressive revolution — architecture and conversation are coupled constraints.
:::

## 8. Expressivity: prosody, style tokens, SSML {#ch8}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Prosody, three continuous sliders]{.tag} The manner of saying decomposes into $F_0$ (melody, in Hz — \~100-200 Hz for men, 160-300 for women, final fall of declarative utterances), *duration* (contrastive lengthening: a stretched "énorme"), *energy* (accents, stressed words). These sliders are *continuous and intertwined*: the TTS must predict them all, and text alone is ambiguous (one neutral sentence, ten valid readings) — it is the one-to-many of ch. 7, aesthetic version. French adds its signature: *final* group accent (not lexical as in English), interrogative rise without inversion, sustained rate that makes segmentation critical.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 8.2 — Global Style Tokens (Wang et al., Interspeech 2018): style as a controllable latent]{.tag} A *reference encoder* reads a reference audio (a few seconds) and produces an embedding; an attention reads this embedding over a *bank of style tokens* (small learned dictionary of "manners of saying"); the weighted vector conditions the Tacotron (rendezvous of ch. 7). Three uses: *transfer* (give the audio of an enthusiastic speaker, generate the target text with their prosody), *control* (move the embedding in token space — attenuate "aggressive"), *exploration* (the tokens spontaneously organize into interpretable axes: rate, energy, emotion). It is the steering vector of the Control module (M2) ch. 4, applied to TTS: a latent direction read from contrasts, added instead of learned — same virtues (soft, composable control), same limits (no guarantee).
:::

::: def
[Definition 8.3 — SSML: the hard control of production]{.tag} The *Speech Synthesis Markup Language* (W3C) is the control language of industrial TTS: pauses (`<break time="500ms"/>`), rate/pitch (`<prosody rate="+10%" pitch="+2st">`), emphasis (`<emphasis>`), pronunciation (`<phoneme alphabet="ipa" ph="ʁə.ʒan">`), dates and numbers. It is a **hard constraint** in the sense of the Control module ch. 2: the engine is *obliged* to obey (exact pause), as opposed to the soft conditioning of style tokens. **Text normalization** (front-end): "1 234 567 €" $\to$ "un million deux cent trente-quatre mille cinq cent soixante-sept euros" is the hidden half of TTS — neural systems integrate the front-end (letter tokenizer) at the price of amusing errors (acronyms, "SARS-CoV-2": to be tested in lab 2).
:::

::: note
[Controlling what, and how: the complete grid]{.tag} Chapter recap in the taxonomy of the Control module (M2):

  Target         Soft mechanism                          Hard mechanism
  -------------- --------------------------------------- -------------------------------
  Voice          speaker embedding (ch. 9)               per-speaker model (fine-tune)
  Prosody        style tokens, audio prompt (Voicebox)   SSML prosody/phoneme
  Segmentation   duration predictor                      SSML break, max length
  Content        LLM upstream (referral to LLMs M2)      pronunciation lexicon

In production: the two columns coexist — SSML for precision (announcements, accessibility), latents for naturalness (conversation).
:::

## 9. Voice conversion and cloning: ethics and watermarking {#ch9}

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Conversion, adaptation, zero-shot cloning]{.tag} *Voice conversion*: re-emit *what* a source voice says *with the timbre* of a target voice (content preserved, speaker changed). *Zero-shot cloning*: synthesize *any text* in a given voice from an *audio prompt* of a few seconds (VALL-E, Voicebox: conditioning by reference, ch. 7). Technically: a speaker embedding (learned by speaker verification — the GE2E loss of Wan et al., 2018, aligns the embeddings of the same voice); YourTTS (ICML 2022) adds it to VITS (the TTS of ch. 7 becomes multi-speaker in one training); VALL-E (Microsoft, 2023) treats cloning as language: AR over the EnCodec *acoustic tokens* (ch. 11), the 3 s prompt serving as prefix — TTS is absorbed by the LLM paradigm.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — Ethics: the law follows (slowly), the engineer decides (fast)]{.tag} Cloning from 3 s of reference makes possible: voice fraud (calls to the "boss"), audio disinformation, impersonation. Frameworks: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act, art. 50) imposes *transparency* — systems generating or manipulating image/voice must mark their outputs machine-readably; in France, the voice is protected as an attribute of personality (civil case law on imitation). For the engineer, the operational answer is technical: *consent* (voice datasets under a clear license — lab 2 uses only authorized voices), *marking* (watermarking, below), *detection* (provenance: cf. Explainability module ch. 9 for text, the logic is identical). The exam question: "why is TTS watermarking *easier* than text watermarking?" — because the output space is continuous and the channel capacity is immense (ch. 6): one can hide bits without perceptible loss... but the channel degrades under compressions.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.3 — Audio watermarking: from spread spectrum to networks]{.tag} *Classical*: spread-spectrum tattooing — add a low-energy pseudo-random noise (key $k$), masked by the psychoacoustic threshold effect, in a time-frequency domain (STFT — Signal Processing M1 modules ch. 6-7: time-frequency analysis and random signals are proven there); detection by correlation with the key — the *exact* structure of the textual green/red watermark (ch. 6 of the Control module): a pseudo-random key, a hypothesis test, a strength/quality trade-off. *Neural*: **WavMark** (2023) hides \~32 bits per second of speech with a learned encoder/detector, robust to re-encodings; **AudioSeal** (Meta, ICASSP 2024) adds *localization*: a sample-level detector indicates *which* segments are synthetic (adversarial generator/detector, perceptual loss); marking *during* generation (in-generation) applies the watermark in the TTS itself — inseparable from the output. Evaluation protocol: ROC curves detection rate / false positives, under attack (mp3, re-voicing, reverberation) — the robustness budget of the Control module ch. 10, word for word.
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.4 — Voice fraud in 3 steps (and its 3 countermeasures)]{.tag} (1) 3 s of public voice $\to$ zero-shot cloning; (2) urgency script generated by an LLM (referral to LLMs M2); (3) vishing call. Countermeasures: (i) *channel*: automatic call-back on a known number (the most robust control is organizational); (ii) *challenge* posed by the interlocutor (off-script question — conversational TTS answer these better and better, cf. ch. 10); (iii) *provenance*: watermark verified at reception if both phones support it. Moral of the module: no single layer suffices — defense in depth.
:::

## 10. The conversational loop: VAD, turn-taking, full-duplex {#ch10}

::: thm
[Theorem 10.1 — The human speaking turn, in numbers]{.tag} Human conversation alternates turns with a median delay on the order of 200 ms — measured across a dozen languages (Stivers et al., PNAS 2009); now pronouncing the first word of a turn takes \~600 ms: humans *anticipate* the end of the other's turn (prosodic, syntactic, pragmatic cues) to prepare their own. An assistant that listens to everything, waits for silence, transcribes, thinks, synthesizes, shows \~1.5-3 s of latency — *five to ten times too slow*: turn-taking is the real conversational bottleneck, not intelligence. Reference framework: the survey by Skantze (Computer Speech & Language, 2021): transition-relevance points (TRP), end-of-turn prediction (end-of-turn: classifier on a sliding window — VAD + prosody + syntax), *backchannels* ("hmm", audible nods: listening without taking the turn).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 10.2 — Pipeline: endpointing as control]{.tag} Deciding "the user is done" is an error/latency trade-off: cutting too early = interruptions (the assistant speaks *over* — the most badly perceived error), cutting too late = dead silences. Parameters: silence threshold $\tau_s$ (typically 300-700 ms), depth of context (rising prosody? incomplete syntax?), and *policy* (letting long hesitations speak). Formalization: a sequential test — detect the "end of turn" regime change as early as possible under a false-positive constraint; the same fidelity/cost curve as streaming ASR (ch. 5), this time at the *dialogue* level. Modern implementation: the end-of-turn predictor becomes a small *multi-modal* model (audio + partial text) that replaces hand-tuned thresholds.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 10.3 — Full-duplex: dGSLM then Moshi (the 2023-2024 leap)]{.tag} **dGSLM** (Nguyen et al., TACL 2023): the first *entirely vocal* dialogue model — two streams of HuBERT tokens (discretized speech, ch. 11) run in parallel; the model learns *by itself* alternation and overlaps (simultaneous laughs): proof of concept that turn-taking is *learnable* without text. **Moshi** (Défossez et al., Kyutai, 2024): the first real-time full-duplex voice assistant. Three pieces: (i) the neural codec *Mimi* (descendant of EnCodec, ch. 11) tokenizes audio at low rate (\~12.5 frames/s) into two streams: semantic and acoustic; (ii) the *multi-stream* architecture: the tokens of *Moshi* (the model's voice) and of the *user* are predicted *in parallel*, not in alternation — the model can cut itself off or fall silent during an interruption; (iii) the *inner monologue*: each audio token of the model is aligned with its corresponding *text* token — the text guides, the audio realizes; theoretical latency \~200 ms (the human target of thm. 10.1), dialogue memory via the transformer context. The module's loop is closed: VAD, endpointing, ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline *disappear* into a single generative model — the next topic.
:::

::: note
[What full-duplex changes in practice]{.tag} (i) *Interruptions*: handled natively (the user stream continues to be predicted while Moshi speaks — the model "hears itself" speak); (ii) *Backchannels*: emergent, unscripted; (iii) *The voice of machines*: unique and marked vocal identity (transparency policy — AI Act ch. 9); (iv) *the risk*: human latency makes the machine socially *indistinguishable* — watermarking (ch. 9) becomes the only frontier. To be debated in session: should a 200 ms assistant announce itself?
:::

## 11. Speech LLMs and multilingualism {#ch11}

::: def
[Definition 11.1 — Tokenizing audio: neural codecs and RVQ]{.tag} A neural *codec* (EnCodec: Défossez et al., 2022) compresses speech with a convolutional auto-encoder constrained by a **residual vector quantization** (RVQ): the continuous latent is approximated by a sum of vectors from successive codebooks — each frame (at 24 kHz: one frame $\approx$ 320 samples, \~75 Hz) becomes a stack of \~2-32 discrete indices. Result: speech becomes a *text* of tokens — consumable by a transformer. The hierarchy of **AudioLM** (Borsos et al., 2023) orders these tokens: first *semantic* (discretized units of a self-supervised model — wav2vec 2/HuBERT — that capture the content), then *coarse* then *fine acoustic* (timbre, environment): generating in this order guarantees the content before the texture. It is the architecture of dGSLM and Moshi (ch. 10).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 11.2 — Speech LLMs: three audio grafts onto an LLM]{.tag}

1.  **Audio-in**: the speech encoder (Whisper, HuBERT) is projected into the LLM's space by an adapter (SALMONN, SpeechGPT, and all multimodal assistants 2025+) — the model *listens* (implicit transcription, paralinguistics: emotion, speaker) and answers in text; it is the "audio-in" family of ch. 8 of the LLMs module (M2), same machinery as vision;
2.  **Audio-out**: the LLM generates *acoustic tokens* (VALL-E: AR over EnCodec with a voice prompt; AudioLM units at the output); the cloning of ch. 9 becomes a skill of the language model;
3.  **Audio-in-out (speech-to-speech)**: Moshi (ch. 10): the text is the *inner monologue* guiding the audio tokens in both directions — the LLM *is* the pipeline. SpeechT5 (2022) had laid down the first unified text/speech architecture (T5 encoder-decoder + shared codebook); 2024-2026 generalize: one model, all the module's tasks (ASR, TTS, speech translation, editing, voice to voice).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 11.3 — Multilingualism: 7,000 languages, 100 covered]{.tag} The bottleneck of low-resource languages: labeling is expensive, writing is sometimes lacking. **MMS** (Meta, 2023 — "Scaling Speech Technology to 1000+ Languages"): a single wav2vec 2 model covers 1,107 languages in ASR *and* TTS (4,017 in language identification), learned on public religious readings (the paradox: the bible is the most translated corpus in the world) — a jump by a factor of 10-40 in coverage. **Common Voice** (Mozilla): open crowd-sourcing (including French — regional accents: lab 1 draws from it). The specificities of French return (ch. 4, ex. 4.3): number normalization (the date sub-test: "en 1996"), acronyms, loanwords. For the engineer: zero-shot (Whisper/MMS) first, light adaptation next (LoRA on the encoder — LLMs module M2 ch. 6), targeted data last; and measure *per language* — a multilingual "average" WER masks local collapses.
:::

::: note
[Conclusion of the module — the fusion of the three worlds]{.tag} Signal (M1), language (LLMs M2), conversation (this module): speech is no longer an interface *in front of* language, it becomes one of its dialects — discrete tokens like any others, generatable, guidable, controllable. The control of the *Control in Generative AI* module (M2, ch. 2: the taxonomy) now applies word for word: hard constraints = SSML and prosody grammars; guidance = style tokens and cloning by prompt; watermarking = voice provenance (ch. 9); evaluation = WER/MOS/latency and trade-off curves. Wherever you set foot in 2026 — research or product — the final question is the same: *what must be controlled, and at what price?*
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Lab: Whisper transcription and WER (the module's ASR lab).** With `transformers`: (a) load `openai/whisper-tiny` as an ASR pipeline, transcribe two French excerpts from Common Voice (one read, one spontaneous); (b) implement the WER (word-level Levenshtein alignment: $S + D + I$ against the reference); (c) compare tiny/small; (d) pre-filter with Silero VAD (cut the silences) and measure the effect on the hallucinations of (a); (e) redo on English to situate French.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): tiny is 2-3× faster but clearly more fragile; the spontaneous French WER is 1.5-3× read English; the VAD massively reduces the hallucinated loops on silences (Whisper "invents" text without energy — prop. 4.2 experienced); beware of normalizations (capitalization, punctuation: normalize before aligning, otherwise the WER is artifactual). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **Lab: TTS with transformers (the synthesis lab).** (a) synthesize a French text with a public TTS model (SpeechT5; French MMS-TTS); (b) measure the RTF (computation time / audio duration) and the first-sample latency; (c) try three trap sentences: "1 234 567 €", "le SARS-CoV-2", "à Saint-Étienne, il est 19 h58" — record the normalization failures; (d) inject a different speaker embedding and compare.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: RTF $<$ 1 on GPU, on the order of 1-3 on CPU; the first-sound latency is dominated by the length of the first Mel *chunk*; numbers and acronyms fail reproducibly — discuss neural vs rule-based front-end (def. 8.3); the embedding shifts the timbre but not the regional accent: perfect zero-shot cloning does not exist with a single vector (ch. 9: one needs the sequential prompt, VALL-E style). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **CTC by hand.** Take up example 2.2 ($T = 4$, $y = \texttt{ab}$): with $p_t(\epsilon) = 0.5$, $p_t(a) = 0.3$, $p_t(b) = 0.2$ for $t = 1..4$, compute the 8 products, sum them, check that the sum equals the $\alpha_4(4) + \alpha_4(3)$ obtained by the recursions of Theorem 2.3 (fill in the $\alpha$ table row by row).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the $\alpha$ table has 4 rows $\times$ 5 columns (with structural zeros — one cannot reach $\ell_4$ before $t=2$); most probable path among the 8: the one that maximizes each column; check that the bound $T \geq \|y\|$ (here 2) is necessary and explain the jump condition $\mathbf 1\{\ell_s \neq \ell_{s-2}\}$ on a counter-example "aa". [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **CTC in code, gradient verified.** Implement $\alpha$, $\beta$ (thm. 2.3) in NumPy for a mini-vocabulary; compute $\partial \mathcal L/\partial p_t(k)$ by the closed formula; check against automatic differentiation (autograd/PyTorch of the sum of paths) to within $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$.

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the convention ($\beta$ with or without the $p_t$ factor) is the classic error — the autograd check detects it immediately; measured complexity $\mathcal O(T S)$ versus enumeration (8 paths here: explodes beyond $T = 15$); conclude on the differentiation *of the full model's objective* (softmax + recursions) — this is exactly what PyTorch does, vectorized. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **Latency budget of a voice assistant.** A pipeline: VAD (30 ms window) $\to$ chunking ASR (640 ms chunk, 160 ms lookahead) $\to$ LLM (time-to-first-token 250 ms) $\to$ TTS (first Mel chunk 120 ms + vocoder 20 ms). (a) compute the first-sound latency of the response (component-by-component detail); (b) identify the two dominant terms and propose three reductions; (c) compare with Moshi's full-duplex (\~200 ms theoretical): what does it remove?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: (a) $\approx 160$ (endpointing to add: silence threshold 300-500 ms! the real cost) $+$ (640+160)$\times$1/80 Hz… take care of the units: the audio chunk counts in seconds, not frames; total typically 1-2 s of which half is endpointing; (b) reduce the threshold by end-of-turn prediction (prop. 10.2), ASR with a smaller chunk, speculative LLM (referral to LLMs M2 ch. 6); (c) Moshi removes VAD/endpointing (continuous stream prediction), ASR/TTS (native audio tokens) and the LLM queue: what remains is network time + one model step. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **Audio watermarking: ROC under attack (bonus).** Synthesize 20 sentences (lab 2); mark half of them with a public audio watermark (e.g. AudioSeal); plot the detector's ROC (true positive / false positive) on: clean audio, mp3 re-encoding at 64 kbps, light noise addition; conclude on the end-to-end provenance channel (ch. 9).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the clean curve is nearly perfect (AUC $>$ 0.99); mp3 degrades moderately (the watermark survives usual compressions — it is designed for that); strong additive noise attacks harder; relate to the robustness budget (Control module ch. 10): marking strength $\uparrow$ = imperceptibility $\downarrow$ — the same triple trade-off as in text. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
